overview: This file brings together U.S. diplomatic and military reporting from 1940–1944 on Japanese propaganda, espionage, recruitment, collaboration, and alleged sabotage in wartime China. Its contents range from original Chinese-language leaflets and translations of air-dropped propaganda to intelligence profiles of suspected agents, descriptions of Japanese networks in Qingdao and Nanjing, reports on operations attributed to General Kenji Doihara, and investigations of individual collaborators. Collectively, the documents trace Japan’s efforts to weaken Chinese and Allied resistance through pan-Asian rhetoric, anti-Western appeals, intimidation, disinformation, covert recruitment, and intelligence gathering during the Second Sino-Japanese and Pacific Wars.
interest: The file is especially useful because it preserves both propaganda artifacts and the American bureaucratic records that interpreted, translated, circulated, and acted upon them. The leaflets reveal how Japan adapted messages for different audiences—Chinese civilians, overseas Chinese, and British defenders—by combining promises of Asian liberation with threats, exaggerated Allied losses, and claims of Western abandonment. Reports on suspected spies and collaborators also illuminate the uncertain evidentiary world of wartime intelligence, while the use of Lin Yu-t’ang’s writing shows how texts could be selectively repurposed across political and national boundaries.
